newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela quake toll rises as rescuers comb ruins.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela quake toll rises as rescuers comb ruins.

text.p: Using their bare hands to heave aside rubble, rescuers in eastern Venezuela on Thursday searched for dozens of children trapped under rubble left by a powerful quake that killed at least 59 people.
"The total number of deaths confirmed now is 59, with 322 injured," Sucre State Governor Ramon Martinez told reporters.

Schools and office buildings were razed by the tremor -- measured at 6.9 on the Richter scale -- crushing children in their classrooms and workers in their offices. Authorities said the death toll could rise.
Many of the pupils were taking end-of-term exams when the quake struck.
Victims ranged from infants to the elderly. Another 500 families were left homeless by the South American nation's worst earthquake for three decades.
President Rafael Caldera announced three days of national mourning. He was due to inspect the rescue operation on Thursday afternoon.
More than 20 hours after the first tremor, survivors were being pulled from rubble.

The small agricultural town Cariaco about 295 miles (470 km) east of Caracas, took the brunt of the disaster. Scores of homes and buildings were flattened, including two schools, killing at least 41, mostly children.
"The problem is very serious. The high school building fell to the ground and there were many children in classes," Martinez told reporters.
Dozens of distraught family members milled in the street facing the Raimundo Martinez Centeno high school, staring blankly as rescue workers searched.
Textbooks and broken desks lay scattered. Several limbs could be seen in the bloodied rubble.

For many of the pupils Thursday was due to be their last day before the summer break. "Some of them were taking end of term exams," said arts teacher Tomas Pantoja as he tried to rescue a student marked with crippling wounds to his legs and arms.
About 500 pupils were inside when the building crashed to the ground, Pantoja said. "The building collapsed as if it had been hit by a bomb," he said.
Jhonny Delgado, a fourth grade student, said he escaped through a hole in the rubble after sitting out the first tremor that lasted about 10 seconds.
In the historic state capital Cumana 40 miles (60 km) west, rescue efforts were concentrated on a six-story office building that fell like a pack of cards.
Martinez said at least 11 bodies were pulled from the ruins and another 30 rescued alive.
"We don't know how many people are still in there but we know there are a lot because the quake hit during office hours," Jose Azocar, Cumana's fire chief, told reporters.
Firemen and medics swarmed over the rubble, removing debris and trying to keep contact with those buried. Cranes and trucks stood by to remove the rubble.
Around dawn on Thursday a group clustered near one of the holes opened in the wreckage burst into cheers and applause. Shortly afterwards a woman was carried away on a stretcher.
One group of survivors, trapped in the basement, kept in contact with the outside world by cellular telephones, Martinez said.
Up to 70 people were thought to have been in the building at the time of the quake.
Hospitals were overwhelmed by the flood of injured.

"Most of those hurt were children and have lost their legs and arms after they were taken from the ruins and then given very rudimentary surgery," said Ramon Ward, director of Cariaco's 30-bed Diego Carbonel hospital which has treated hundreds of patients since Wednesday afternoon.
"Some died bleeding on their way to the hospital," he added.
Mayor Miguel Vasquez said the agricultural town of 13,000 was destroyed by the quake; streets were riven by huge cracks and houses flattened.

The quake, the worst to hit Venezuela since 1967, struck about 3:25 p.m. EDT (1925 GMT) on Wednesday, sending panicked people into the streets in cities and towns from the capital to the furthest eastern tip of the country.
The FUNVISIS seismological institute said the first quake measured 6.9 on the open-ended Richter scale.

The epicentre was about 30 miles (49 km) off Venezuela's northeastern Caribbean coast and there were 15 aftershocks, the last in the early hours of Thursday, they said. FUNVISIS warned that further aftershocks could occur.
State-owned oil company Petroleos de Venezuela said production and export continued to flow smoothly. Venezuela is the largest exporter of crude oil to the United States.

Founded in 1521, Cumana is the oldest inhabited city in South America. However, most of its colonial architecture was destroyed in a massive earthquake in 1766. Wednesday's earthquake was the second major tremor to strike the city of 250,000 people this century, the last in 1929.
The 1967 quake, the last to cause serious damage in Venezuela, killed 215 in the capital and surrounding area, FUNVISIS officials said.
